entries.clue: Principally revere a saint that’s rejected Russian despot (4)

indicatorNotes.Principally: What matters principally is what comes first, so only the opening letter of each word that follows is taken.
indicatorNotes.rejected: To reject a thing is to throw it back, and letters thrown back arrive in the opposite order.

blocks.note: The opening letter of each of these four words, in the order the clue prints them.

annotation.surface: Worship offered to a saint the church has turned away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Principally' reads in the sentence as an adverb of degree — mainly revering — and is really an instruction to collect initials. 'Rejected' then sends what it collected the other way.
annotation.definitionFit: A tsar was the emperor of Russia, ruling by his own word and answerable to nobody, which is what despot says of a ruler.

entries.clue: Went both sides of alders sprayed with DDT (9)

indicatorNotes.sprayed: A spray scatters what it carries in every direction, so the letters land in no order of their own.

blocks.note: Six of the nine letters to be re-set.
The pesticide's three letters go into the mix as they stand.

annotation.surface: A stand of alder trees getting a dousing of insecticide.
annotation.walkthrough: DDT is fodder, not an abbreviation waiting to be decoded, and it is the only part of the clue in capitals. Nine letters is a long shuffle, so the crossings usually arrive first.
annotation.definitionFit: To straddle something is to stand with a leg on either side of it, so having straddled it is having gone both sides of it at once.

entries.clue: Cricket score coming at no cost: go wild! (3,4)

blocks.note: The single point in cricket, scored by the batters crossing between the wickets.
What comes at no cost comes free.

annotation.surface: Runs arriving for nothing, and a crowd told to celebrate.
annotation.walkthrough: Cricket gives the crossword its commonest small words — a run, an over, a duck — and this clue wants the plainest of them. The exclamation mark warns that the definition is a phrase rather than a single word.
annotation.definitionFit: To run free is to be let loose with nothing holding you back, which is the going wild the clue's exclamation asks for.

entries.clue: Everyman, alternately canny and stingy (4)

indicatorNotes.alternately: To do something alternately is to do it every other time, so every second letter of the word is used and the rest dropped.

blocks.note: Everyman sets this puzzle, so the name is the setter pointing at their own self.
The second and fourth letters of the word, kept in order.

annotation.surface: The setter described as shrewd one moment and tight-fisted the next.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter who signs the puzzle can drop that signature into a clue and mean themselves by it — a convention worth owning early. 'Alternately' looks like it is contrasting two adjectives and is counting letters instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Mean is the everyday British word for unwilling to part with money, which is exactly what stingy says of a person.

entries.clue: Dreamboat didn’t follow directions, you say (2,5)

indicatorNotes.you say: 'You say' points at speech rather than print, so the phrase is wanted for its sound and not for its spelling.

blocks.note: Not following a direction is missing it, and the direction missed here is right.

annotation.surface: Somebody who ignored the route they were given.
annotation.walkthrough: The plural 'directions' is the cover: only one of them, right, ends up in the sound. Said at speed, 'missed right' collapses its first word to two letters, and what comes out on the page is a title.
annotation.definitionFit: Mr Right is the standing name for the perfect partner somebody is waiting to meet, which is what calling a man a dreamboat says of him.

entries.clue: Kindle Crime? (5)

blocks.note: The capital K offers the e-reader; the setter means the plain old verb, to set something alight.
On the device it is a shelf of thrillers to browse, and in the answer it is the offence itself.

annotation.surface: Browsing the crime titles on an e-reader.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words and a capital letter are the whole clue. Amazon named the Kindle after kindling a fire, and the setter is quietly borrowing that sense back.
annotation.definitionFit: Arson is the criminal offence of deliberately setting fire to property, so kindling something on purpose is precisely the crime being named.

entries.clue: Thing – or have a thing (6)

blocks.note: Any item you can point at and pick up.
To have a thing about something is to mind it, and to say so out loud.

annotation.surface: An item on offer, or a strong feeling about one.
annotation.walkthrough: The word 'thing' does both jobs, which is the joke: once as the noun the answer is, once inside the idiom the answer's verb means. The dash is a divider and nothing more.
annotation.definitionFit: An object is a thing you can handle, and to object is to have a thing about something — to register that you mind it.

entries.clue: Crossword setter’s stock-in-trade: con game (6)

blocks.note: What a setter turns out all day, and what you are reading at this moment.
To do somebody is to swindle them, the sense in being done out of money.

annotation.surface: A crossword compiler's working materials, and a confidence trick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Con game' reads as one phrase, a swindle, and the split falls between its two words. The first half of the clue describes the sentence it is printed in, which is the setter's wink at the solver.
annotation.definitionFit: Cluedo is the British board game of murder in the library with the candlestick, sold as Clue in North America.

entries.clue: Return ball-dress after alterations for philosopher (8,7)

indicatorNotes.after alterations: Alterations take a garment apart and sew it back a different shape, so the same letters come back in a different order.

blocks.note: Fifteen letters off the three printed words, re-set.

annotation.surface: Sending a gown back to the shop to be taken in.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'ball-dress' does nothing but make the fodder look like one garment, and 'Return' is fodder too rather than a reversal instruction. Russell wrote the Principia Mathematica with Whitehead and won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
annotation.definitionFit: Bertrand Russell was the British philosopher and logician who dominated the first half of the twentieth century, as famous for his campaigning as for his logic.

entries.clue: Obese superhero’s sidekick’s getting letters from many (5,6)

blocks.note: A round figure is a well-padded one.
Batman's young partner is Robin, and the clue's second apostrophe-s hands over the final letter.

annotation.surface: A well-fed young assistant to a caped hero, going through the post.
annotation.walkthrough: That second apostrophe-s is fodder rather than grammar — it is what makes the plural. A round robin is a letter circulated along a list or signed by everybody on it.
annotation.definitionFit: A round robin goes round a whole group and comes back signed by all of them, so it really does arrive as letters from many.

entries.clue: Wronged: then can’t men appeal? (11)

indicatorNotes.Wronged: To be wronged is to be put wrong, and letters put wrong are letters no longer standing where they belong.

blocks.note: Eleven letters off these three words, re-set.

annotation.surface: A grumble that men who have been wronged are given no right of appeal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Appeal' closes a sentence about injustice and looks like the legal kind; the sense wanted is charm. Nothing here is abbreviated — all eleven letters come straight off the page.
annotation.definitionFit: Enchantment is the spell a person or a place casts over you, and appeal is that same pull described without the magic.

entries.clue: Relaxed educator spending time somewhere in S America (7)

indicatorNotes.Relaxed: Something relaxed has loosened its grip, so the letters are no longer held in the order they arrived in.
indicatorNotes.spending: To spend a thing is to part with it, so that letter is paid away before the rest is used.

blocks.note: The eight letters of the word less that T, leaving seven to re-set.
T is the standing abbreviation for time, and it is what gets spent.

annotation.surface: A teacher taking time off and unwinding a long way from home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Relaxed' and 'spending' are both instructions wearing the clothes of a teacher's holiday. Knock the T out first: shuffling eight letters and losing one afterwards is the slow way round.
annotation.definitionFit: Ecuador is the South American republic on the Pacific coast, named after the equator that runs across it.

entries.clue: Grand, skipping starter of zest and truffle mixture (7)

indicatorNotes.skipping starter of: To skip a thing is to leave it out, and a word's starter is the letter it begins with, so that first letter never appears.

blocks.note: G is the standing abbreviation for grand.
Zest in the sense of dash and flair is panache, and the skipped starter is its P.

annotation.surface: A grand dinner where the zesty starter is skipped for the truffles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starter' is a course on the surface and a first letter in the wordplay, while 'zest' is the flair kind rather than the lemon kind. Ganache is chocolate melted into cream, the soft centre a truffle is rolled from.
annotation.definitionFit: Ganache is the chocolate-and-cream paste that is chilled, rolled and dusted to make a truffle, so it is the mixture a truffle is made of.

entries.clue: Slurred ‘Let’s did it!’ being most tipsy (9)

indicatorNotes.Slurred: Slurred speech runs its sounds into one another so the word comes out the wrong shape, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: Nine letters off the quoted words, re-set.

annotation.surface: A drunk mangling a boast about what the night involved.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the giveaway: 'Let's did it' is not English, and ungrammatical wording inside quotes is almost always fodder. Tiddly is the mild British word for slightly drunk.
annotation.definitionFit: Tiddly is the gentle British term for tipsy, so its superlative names whoever in the room is furthest gone.

entries.clue: I’m next to Charlie, hurrah! (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The first half is not a synonym at all: the answer speaks in its own voice and names its place in the radio alphabet instead of describing something else.

blocks.note: In the NATO radio alphabet the codeword for B is the one read out immediately before Charlie's C.
The shout thrown from the stalls when the aria lands.

annotation.surface: Standing beside a friend called Charlie and cheering.
annotation.walkthrough: Charlie is the crossword's usual flag for the radio alphabet, where every letter has a fixed word and the order never changes. Neither half of this clue is wordplay: both simply name the same five letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The NATO codeword for B sits directly before Charlie in the alphabet, and the same word is the cry of approval shouted at a performer.

entries.clue: Voracious fish finding something to chew: American by Hebridean island (9)

indicatorNotes.by: To sit by a thing is to sit at its side, and here it is the island that is sat beside, so the island's letters come first and the rest settle after them.

blocks.note: Barra is one of the Outer Hebrides off the west coast of Scotland, known for the beach its aeroplanes land on.
Cud is the half-digested mouthful a cow brings back up to work on again.
A is the standing abbreviation for American.

annotation.surface: A hungry fish hunting for a mouthful off the Scottish coast.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay is printed back to front — what the clue names last stands first in the grid. Barra will not be in many heads, so the crossings and the fish are what get you there.
annotation.definitionFit: The barracuda is the long, fast, sharp-toothed predator of warm seas, notorious for tearing into anything that moves near it.

entries.clue: Lived with Rose (5)

blocks.note: Put up with — having tolerated somebody's company rather than having shared an address.
Got up out of a chair; the capital is there only to make it look like a name.

annotation.surface: Somebody recalling the years they spent sharing a house with Rose.
annotation.walkthrough: Rose takes a capital and looks like the person being lived with, and it is the past tense of a verb. Both halves are past tense, which is the check that two definitions really answer the same word.
annotation.definitionFit: To stand something is to put up with it, so having lived with it is having stood it; and whoever got to their feet stood.

entries.clue: That woman embracing excessively rising calm (6)

indicatorNotes.embracing: An embrace closes the arms right round somebody, so the word doing it wraps itself round the letters that follow.
indicatorNotes.rising: A down entry is written from the top of the grid downwards, so letters that are rising are read the other way, from the foot upwards.

blocks.note: The pronoun for a woman already mentioned.
Too loud, too long — the little word that means excessively.

annotation.surface: A woman whose hug goes on rather longer than it should.
annotation.walkthrough: The three-letter pronoun splits one letter to two, which is a shape worth expecting whenever a short word is asked to embrace something. 'Excessively' is the plain adverb, not a hint that anything is overdone.
annotation.definitionFit: To soothe someone is to calm them down, and both verbs take an object in exactly the same way.

entries.clue: Al Gore is the MC, repeatedly failing to finish instructions (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is plural and the answer singular: an algorithm is one named thing made of a sequence of instructions, so the plural noun stands for the set the word names.

indicatorNotes.repeatedly failing to finish: Failing to finish means stopping before the last letter, and 'repeatedly' says the same stopping happens to each of the four things in turn.

blocks.note: The former US vice-president's two names run together and cut one letter short.
The word again stopped before its last letter.
Same treatment: the word without its final letter.
An MC is the master of ceremonies, and only the first of the two letters survives.

annotation.surface: Al Gore compering an evening and never quite getting to the end of anything.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Repeatedly' is the only warning that one operation applies four separate times. Even 'is' and 'the' are fodder here, which is what makes the clue read as an ordinary sentence right up to the last word.
annotation.definitionFit: An algorithm is the step-by-step procedure a computer is set to follow, which is a set of instructions written out in order.

entries.clue: Mature years welcoming: Vera and Norm (7)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: To welcome someone is to take them in, so the word doing the welcoming opens up and the guest goes inside it.

blocks.note: Somebody's mature years are their age, and to mature is to age.
The woman's name, taken straight off the page.

annotation.surface: An elderly couple called Vera and Norm being made welcome.
annotation.walkthrough: Norm reads as a man's name standing beside Vera, and it is the definition. Only one of the two names is fodder; the other carries the meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: An average is the normal or typical value of a set, so norm is the same idea in one syllable.

entries.clue: Good boy, Warren? Cheer up (7)

blocks.note: G is the standing abbreviation for good.
A lad is a boy, chiefly in British use.
A warren is a rabbit's home, and the question mark owns up to the broader word being asked for.

annotation.surface: A pep talk delivered to somebody called Warren.
annotation.walkthrough: Warren takes a capital and reads as a first name — Warren Beatty, Warren Buffett — which is the only thing standing between the solver and three easy chunks. The question mark is the setter admitting the animal's home is not exactly the one named.
annotation.definitionFit: To gladden someone is to make them glad, which is what cheering them up amounts to.

entries.clue: Sir and Madam I stereotype to an extent (6)

indicatorNotes.to an extent: Doing a thing to an extent is doing it only partly, so a stretch of these words is wanted rather than the whole of them.

blocks.note: Six letters run end to end here, beginning inside the first word and finishing inside the last.

annotation.surface: A complaint that calling people Sir and Madam is a bit of a stereotype.
annotation.walkthrough: The hidden run crosses two word-breaks, which is what hides it — the eye reads whole words and the letters pay them no attention. The two forms of address sit at opposite ends of the clue, one defining and one concealing.
annotation.definitionFit: Mister is the ordinary title for a man, so it answers to sir as the polite way of addressing one.

entries.clue: Some hector if I celebrate opening (7)

indicatorNotes.Some: 'Some' asks for a part and not the whole, so a stretch of the letters that follow is what is wanted.

blocks.note: Seven letters running unbroken across two word-breaks in this phrase.

annotation.surface: People grumbling at somebody for throwing a party on opening night.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hector' looks like the Trojan prince and is the verb, to bully. 'Some' is the instruction rather than a vague quantity of hecklers, which is the one word to get right here.
annotation.definitionFit: An orifice is a mouth or vent in a body or a surface — a hole let into something, which is what an opening is.

entries.clue: Reported little hole in key (5)

indicatorNotes.Reported: Something reported is passed on in speech, so it is the sound of the phrase that counts and not the way it is written.

blocks.note: The small hole punched in a shoe or a sail for a lace to pass through is an eyelet.

annotation.surface: A small hole discovered in a key, according to report.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Key' is the low island of the Florida Keys, not the thing on a keyring — the same word as the Spanish cayo. An eyelet and the answer are said exactly alike and spelt almost entirely differently.
annotation.definitionFit: A key is a low sandy island, the sense preserved in the Florida Keys, and an islet is a small island of precisely that kind.

entries.clue: Rouses, as a snake coiled round head of wombat (7)

indicatorNotes.coiled: A coiled rope has been wound into a heap with no straight line left in it, so the letters lose the order they came in.
indicatorNotes.round: Going round a thing means passing outside it on every side, so the letters just made close round what follows.
indicatorNotes.head of: The head of a word is the letter at its front, so that single letter is what is taken.

blocks.note: The six letters of these two words, coiled into a new order.
The front letter of wombat.

annotation.surface: A snake wound round a wombat's head, bringing it round.
annotation.walkthrough: The little word 'a' is fodder as well as an article — leave it out and the count comes up short. The Australian pairing is pure surface: nothing in the answer is antipodean.
annotation.definitionFit: To awaken someone is to rouse them out of sleep, and both verbs stand here in the third person singular.

entries.clue: Business listing two things enjoyed by Victorian conwoman? (6,3,6)

annotation.definition: Business listing two things enjoyed by Victorian conwoman?

blocks.note: Read as a directory of firms, and meant as the noisy rush of a place where a great deal is going on.

blocks.clueFragment: two things enjoyed by Victorian conwoman?
blocks.note: Her trade is the swindle, and her skirt is held out at the back by a wire frame; the answer names one of each, with a joining word between them.

annotation.surface: A trade directory of everything a Victorian swindler could want.
annotation.walkthrough: There are no letters to move: the clue promises two rhyming nouns with 'and' between them and then describes each one. A bustle is the frame that shaped a Victorian skirt, and a hustle is a con.
annotation.definitionFit: Hustle and bustle is the standing phrase for crowded, noisy activity, which is business in its older sense of busyness.

entries.clue: Fruitfully traded shares evaluated, initially? (4)

indicatorNotes.initially: Taken initially means taken at the very start, so only the first letter of each word counts towards the answer.

blocks.note: The word's own opening letter, nothing abbreviated.
The second word's opening letter.
The third word's opening letter.
The last word's opening letter, and the last letter needed.

annotation.surface: A note that some shares have been traded and valued profitably.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole sentence is the definition as well as the wordplay, which is what an &lit is. Say the four letters as one word and you have the nickname the City itself uses, footsie.
annotation.definitionFit: The FTSE is the Financial Times Stock Exchange index, the running valuation of shares traded in London, so the sentence describes what it does all day.

entries.clue: How some like their screwdrivers tidily arranged (4)

blocks.note: Poured with nothing added — which is a joke, since the drink of that name is vodka already mixed with orange juice.
Lined up straight with nothing out of place.

annotation.surface: A toolbox where the screwdrivers are all laid out properly.
annotation.walkthrough: The drink is vodka and orange juice, so nobody can take one neat; the setter knows it, and that impossibility is where the joke lives. The surface keeps you in the toolbox, where screwdrivers genuinely do get arranged.
annotation.definitionFit: Neat is how a spirit is served when nothing is added to it, and neat is also what orderly looks like, so both halves land on the same four letters.
